My new book, Co-Existence, is out today.  It is a guide to how to live & work in a world where AI is sometimes, but not always, better than you.

(And, for the release, I worked with Opus 5.5 to make a quite interesting experience for the book's website:

A note on demos: AI models are impressive when talking about AI. Ask them to make a music video or a slide deck or an explainer about AI/"themselves" and they will deliver you something creative & unnerving

But ask for the same for a non-AI topic and you can see more rough edges

Outside of whatever is happening in cryptography, I suspect we are going to see more cases where AI progress in seemingly abstract fields has implications for vital technologies that most people did not realize are related.

Gemini 4 Neon one-shots a novel RPG rulebook that is nicely laid-out and illustrated, and with a unique game mechanic...

...but it is about drowned bell towers and echoes and an ancient cataclysm and strange music. Just like most other RPG ideas from most other models. Odd.

It may not last for long, but for now you need some level of expertise in a subject to use AI for novel discoveries. It is just too easy to produce exciting results from the models that fail because you don’t know the checks to run or wider context or can’t “smell” a problem.

Microsoft is such an interesting case. One part on the frontier of AI, to the point where the CEO of AI is warning of the threshold we are crossing, while much of the rest of the organization is the torchbearer for the “AI is a just a  normal technology like any other” camp.

The story here is looking like a story in robotics and 3D design. The latest frontier models have a tremendous general capability for diverse hard problems that we used to think would require specialized models or approaches.

Bitter lesson everywhere.
Two kinds of people: those watching the agent swarm trying to crack P=NP and those watching the agent swarm trying to illegally port the Xbox version of GTA 6 to the PC. Here is the P=NP one:

Walmart is determined not to make the same mistake with agentic commerce that it did with ecommerce. While Amazon is blocking agents, Walmart is embracing them - quite a reversal.

And the new data from Stripe suggests agentic shopping may actually be kicking off & is sticky.

Not that AI discourse has ever been great, but "of course LLMs are good at math" both misses that "good at math" is an *slight* understatement in the context of solving the Reimann Hypothesis & also ignores the fact that LLMs were not actually "good at math" until very recently.
